anchor: Here, where the world is quiet
title: Occasion and place in Poems and Ballads (1866)
short: Published in Poems and Ballads (1866) between 'Dolores' and 'Hesperia'; Swinburne called it a 'brief total pause of passion and of thought'.
body: The poem appeared in Swinburne's scandalous Poems and Ballads (1866), placed between 'Dolores', a litany to a goddess of cruel pleasure, and 'Hesperia', a poem of gentler love. When reviewers attacked the book (John Morley called Swinburne 'the libidinous laureate of a pack of satyrs'), Swinburne replied in Notes on Poems and Reviews that he had deliberately slipped this poem in between the two, to express a moment when the spirit, without hope or fear, 'hungers and thirsts only after the perfect sleep'. So the speaker's weariness is, in part, the exhaustion that follows passion. The opening 'Here' places us at once inside Proserpine's garden in the underworld, a world beyond 'trouble', 'riot' and dreams.

sources.cite: A. C. Swinburne, Notes on Poems and Reviews (1866), Wikisource
Kenneth Haynes, ed., Swinburne: Poems and Ballads & Atalanta in Calydon (Penguin Classics, 2000), notes to 'The Garden of Proserpine'

anchor: Dead winds' and spent waves' riot
title: Stanza and metre
short: Twelve eight-line stanzas rhyming ababcccb in short three-stress lines, with alternating feminine and masculine rhymes and a triple rhyme before the close.
body: Each stanza has eight short lines of three stresses, rhyming ababcccb. The a and c rhymes are feminine (two syllables: 'quiet/riot', 'growing/sowing/mowing'), the b rhymes masculine ('seems/dreams/streams'). The triple feminine rhyme creates a lulling, falling movement, and the delayed b rhyme at line 8 closes each stanza with a firm masculine stress, as if dropping into sleep. Heavy alliteration ('Dead winds' and spent waves' riot', 'Wan waves and wet winds labour') is characteristic of Swinburne, whose music critics have alternately praised and found monotonous. The poem's form enacts its theme: incantatory repetition, little forward motion, a steady descent toward the final 'eternal night'.

title: Proserpine
short: Proserpina (Greek Persephone), daughter of Ceres, carried off by Pluto to be queen of the dead; here goddess of death and endless sleep.
body: Proserpina, the Latin form of Persephone, was the daughter of Ceres (Demeter), goddess of grain. Gathering flowers in Sicily, she was seized by Pluto (Dis, Hades) and taken to the underworld as his queen; because she ate pomegranate seeds there, she must return below for part of each year, which explains winter (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5; Homeric Hymn to Demeter). Milton recalls her as the flower-gatherer 'herself a fairer Flowre' (Paradise Lost 4.269-72). Swinburne omits the springtime return and the grieving mother: his Proserpine is wholly the queen of death, who 'gathers all things mortal' instead of flowers. The 'green grapes' are unripened, never-maturing fruit, appropriate to a realm where nothing grows to completion.

title: doubtful dreams of dreams
short: The world's 'trouble' has faded to the unreality of a dream of a dream, doubly removed from waking life.
body: The first sentence is grammatically elusive: in this place all trouble 'seems' to be only the riot of dead winds and spent waves, recalled in 'doubtful dreams of dreams'. The doubling removes experience twice over from reality, the way storms seem when one is half asleep. 'Doubtful' carries both 'uncertain' and 'faint, indistinct'. The surrounding scene of a 'green field growing / For reaping folk and sowing' is seen from a distance, a 'sleepy world of streams', as though the speaker watches the living world from the borders of death.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'doubtful'

anchor: For men that sow to reap
title: tears and laughter ... sow to reap
short: Weariness with the whole biblical cycle of weeping and laughing, sowing and reaping, and with promises of a hereafter.
body: Stanza 2 lists what the speaker is tired of: 'tears and laughter', recalling Ecclesiastes 3:4 ('A time to weep, and a time to laugh'), and 'what may come hereafter / For men that sow to reap'. The last phrase echoes Galatians 6:7, 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap', a text about moral consequence and judgement after death. Swinburne turns from the Christian promise of reward or punishment to a desire for 'nothing but sleep'. 'Blown buds of barren flowers' (blown = blossomed, also blown away) gives the image of beauty without fruit that runs through the poem.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Ecclesiastes 3:4
Bible (KJV), Galatians 6:7

title: Weak ships and spirits steer
short: Souls on the troubled sea of life drift without knowing their destination; the underworld garden lies beyond their storms.
body: The voyage image is ambiguous: ships and spirits are steered (or steer) through 'wan waves and wet winds', drifting to an unknown end. It suggests both mortal life as a storm-tossed sea and the passage of souls toward death, perhaps recalling the classical crossing of the rivers of the underworld. The point of the stanza is the contrast between 'thither' (where the drifting go, unknowingly) and 'hither' (the speaker's calm garden, where 'no such winds blow'). The very sound of the line, all w-alliteration and weak stresses, mimics aimless drift.

sources.cite: Jerome J. McGann, Swinburne: An Experiment in Criticism (University of Chicago Press, 1972)
Kenneth Haynes, ed., Swinburne: Poems and Ballads & Atalanta in Calydon (Penguin Classics, 2000), notes to 'The Garden of Proserpine'

title: wot not
short: 'Know not': an archaic, biblical-sounding form of the verb 'wit'.
body: 'Wot' is an archaic present tense of 'wit' (Old English witan, to know), familiar to Swinburne's readers from the King James Bible (e.g. Abimelech's 'I wot not who hath done this thing', Genesis 21:26). The line means: those who sail there do not know where they are going. The archaism lends the poem a scriptural cadence that it then uses against Christian hope, a typical Swinburnean move.

anchor: No growth of moor or coppice
title: coppice
short: A thicket of small trees or underwood; the familiar English and Mediterranean landscapes (moor, heather, vine) are absent here.
body: A coppice is a thicket of small trees and shrubs, originally woodland periodically cut back to encourage new growth (Old French copeiz, from couper, to cut). Swinburne lists what does not grow in Proserpine's garden: moorland, woodland, heather (northern, British) and the vine (southern, classical). In their place come only poppies, unripe grapes and rushes. The stanza replaces a living landscape with a botanical inventory of sleep and death.

sources.cite: Representative Poetry Online (ed. P. F. Morgan), 'The Garden of Proserpine', notes

title: bloomless buds of poppies
short: Poppies, source of opium, were sacred to Ceres and to Sleep; here they never open, a vegetation of oblivion.
body: The poppy was associated in antiquity both with Ceres (Demeter), Proserpine's mother, and with sleep and death: Ovid places poppies at the door of the cave of Sleep, where Night gathers their sleep-bringing juice (Metamorphoses 11.605-7). Victorian readers also knew the poppy as the source of opium and laudanum. Swinburne's buds are 'bloomless', never flowering, like the 'blown buds of barren flowers' of stanza 2: the garden's beauty is sterile. The stanza ends with Proserpine crushing fruit 'For dead men deadly wine', an inversion of Bacchus's life-giving vintage.

title: For dead men deadly wine
short: Proserpine presses a wine of oblivion for the dead, a dark counterpart to Bacchic wine and to the Christian cup of eternal life.
body: The only plant that 'blooms or blushes' in the garden is the one Proserpine crushes into wine for the dead. The polyptoton 'dead ... deadly' makes the drink both for the dead and death-bringing. Wine in classical myth is Bacchus's gift of life and ecstasy, and in Christianity the communion wine promises eternal life; Swinburne's underworld vintage offers only forgetfulness, perhaps recalling Lethe, the river of oblivion. Readers may compare the pomegranate seeds Proserpine ate in Hades, which bound her there, though the poem itself never mentions the pomegranate.

title: fruitless fields of corn
short: 'Corn' means grain. The dead sleep in barren fields, like the fruit-losing willows of Persephone's grove in the Odyssey.
body: 'Corn' is the British term for grain generally (wheat, barley), not maize. The dead, 'without name or number', bow like ripe ears and sleep in fields that bear nothing. Homer describes the grove of Persephone at the edge of the underworld, with tall poplars and 'willows that lose their fruit' (Odyssey 10.509-10), an ancient image of sterile vegetation in the realm of the dead. Ceres was the goddess of corn: her daughter's fields are its negation.

anchor: Though one were strong as seven
title: strong as seven ... fair as roses
short: Neither strength nor beauty nor love escapes death; the stanza closes with a flat reversal: 'In the end it is not well'.
body: The stanza runs through the gifts that might seem to defy death: strength ('strong as seven', a proverbial-sounding superlative), beauty ('fair as roses'), and love. Each is cancelled. 'His beauty clouds and closes' compresses fading and the closing of a flower or of eyes. The last two lines pivot on 'well': though love may rest content, in the end 'it is not well'. The phrase reverses the consoling proverb 'All's well that ends well' (the title of Shakespeare's play) and, implicitly, Christian assurances that all shall be well.

sources.cite: Jerome J. McGann, Swinburne: An Experiment in Criticism (University of Chicago Press, 1972)
Kenneth Haynes, ed., Swinburne: Poems and Ballads & Atalanta in Calydon (Penguin Classics, 2000), notes to 'The Garden of Proserpine'

anchor: Nor wake with wings in heaven
title: Nor wake with wings ... Nor weep for pains in hell
short: An explicit denial of both Christian heaven and hell: the dead neither rise as angels nor suffer punishment.
body: These lines state plainly what the poem implies elsewhere: there is no heavenly reward (the winged soul of popular piety) and no hellish torment. For Victorian readers this was among the most shocking aspects of the poem, which offers comfort precisely in the absence of an afterlife. Louis reads Swinburne's poetry as an evolving agnostic theology, here hostile to the Christian God and drawn to classical imagery of death as rest. Compare stanza 11, where the speaker thanks the gods 'That dead men rise up never'.

sources.cite: Margot K. Louis, Swinburne and His Gods: The Roots and Growth of an Agnostic Poetry (McGill-Queen's UP, 1990)
Wikipedia, 'The Garden of Proserpine' (on form, sources and reception)

title: She who gathers all things mortal / With cold immortal hands
short: Proserpine, once the flower-gatherer, now harvests every mortal life; the antithesis mortal/immortal is the poem's centre.
body: Stanza 7 offers the poem's most famous portrait of Proserpine, standing 'beyond porch and portal' (the gates of the underworld) and 'Crowned with calm leaves'. In the myth she was seized while gathering flowers; Swinburne makes her the gatherer of all mortal things, a reaper rather than a picker of blossoms. The chiming 'mortal / immortal' sets human transience against divine permanence, and 'cold' gives her touch the chill of death. Her 'languid lips' are said to be sweeter than those of Love, who fears her: death is eroticised, in keeping with the poem's place after 'Dolores'.

title: Forgets the earth her mother
short: Proserpine forgets Ceres (Demeter), the earth and harvest goddess: in this version she never returns to bring spring.
body: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter the mother's grief for her lost daughter makes the earth barren until Persephone is restored for part of each year, bringing spring. Swinburne's Proserpine 'Forgets the earth her mother', and 'the life of fruits and corn'. Instead of spring following her up, 'spring and seed and swallow' (the swallow, herald of spring) follow her down into the dark. The poem thus cancels the myth's promise of seasonal renewal, which Christian interpreters had long read as a type of resurrection.

title: Red strays of ruined springs
short: The stanza's procession of dead loves, years and dreams ends in strays, scattered leaves or blossoms blown from wrecked springtimes.
body: Stanza 9 is a catalogue of all that drifts 'thither' to Proserpine: withered loves, dead years, 'disastrous things' (ill-starred, from Latin astrum, star), dead dreams, blind buds shaken by snow, wild leaves taken by wind. 'Strays' are things that have wandered or been scattered, here probably red leaves or petals torn from 'ruined springs'. The alliteration of r and the anaphora on 'And all' give the sense of an endless, melancholy procession, the dead of the natural year joining the human dead.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'stray'

anchor: Time stoops to no man's lure
title: Time stoops to no man's lure
short: A falconry metaphor: time, like a hawk, will not swoop down to the bait a falconer swings to recall it.
body: In falconry a hawk 'stoops' when it dives on its prey, and the 'lure' is the bundle of feathers and meat swung by the falconer to call the bird back. Time is a hawk that no human lure can recall or control. The image sharpens the commonplace that time waits for no man. The stanza around it denies certainty even to sorrow ('We are not sure of sorrow, / And joy was never sure') and ends with love itself weeping that 'no loves endure'.

sources.cite: Representative Poetry Online (ed. P. F. Morgan), 'The Garden of Proserpine', notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'stoop'
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'lure'

title: From too much love of living ... Whatever gods may be
short: The poem's best-known stanza: an agnostic thanksgiving that life is finite. Henley's 'Invictus' echoes the phrase 'whatever gods may be'.
body: Freed from 'too much love of living' and from hope and fear, the speakers offer 'brief thanksgiving' not to God but to 'Whatever gods may be', an agnostic formula, for the fact that no life lasts for ever and 'dead men rise up never'. The consolation is close to the Epicurean argument, best known from Lucretius, that death is nothing to us because we will not exist to feel it (De rerum natura 3.830 and following); Swinburne knew the classics well, though the poem does not cite Lucretius. W. E. Henley's 'Invictus' (1888) uses the same phrase in 'I thank whatever gods may be', with a defiant rather than a weary turn. The stanza was widely quoted and set to music.

sources.cite: Lucretius, De rerum natura 3.830-869 (Perseus Digital Library)
Margot K. Louis, Swinburne and His Gods: The Roots and Growth of an Agnostic Poetry (McGill-Queen's UP, 1990)
Wikipedia, 'Invictus' (text of Henley's poem)

title: the weariest river / Winds somewhere safe to sea
short: Life as a river reaching rest in the sea, with an echo of Ecclesiastes 1:7, 'All the rivers run into the sea'.
body: The image of life as a river ending in the sea is ancient, and the Preacher of Ecclesiastes uses the endless flow of rivers into the sea as an emblem of the weary cycle of things (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Swinburne makes the sea not a place of further labour but safety and rest; 'winds' (meanders) suggests the slow, tired course of a long life. The line is among the most quoted in Victorian poetry. Its relief is the reverse of the drifting ships of stanza 3, which do not know where they are going.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Ecclesiastes 1:7
Kenneth Haynes, ed., Swinburne: Poems and Ballads & Atalanta in Calydon (Penguin Classics, 2000), notes to 'The Garden of Proserpine'

title: diurnal
short: 'Daily': all things that belong to the cycle of day and night will cease, along with the seasons ('wintry ... vernal').
body: 'Diurnal' (Latin diurnalis, from dies, day) means daily, or belonging to the day. Paired with 'wintry leaves nor vernal' (vernal = of spring, Latin ver), it abolishes both the daily and the yearly cycles of time. English readers would recall Wordsworth's 'Rolled round in earth's diurnal course' ('A slumber did my spirit seal'), another poem of death as absorption into the impersonal. The Latinate words lend the final stanza a liturgical solemnity.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'diurnal'
William Wordsworth, 'A slumber did my spirit seal' (1800), l. 7

title: the sleep eternal / In an eternal night
greek: Latin nox est perpetua una dormienda (Catullus 5.6)
short: The closing lines recall Catullus 5: once our brief light sets, 'one perpetual night must be slept'.
body: The poem ends with the eternal sleep its speaker has longed for since stanza 2. The cadence recalls Catullus 5.4-6, where the poet urges Lesbia to love because suns may set and rise again, but for us, once our brief light has set, there is one perpetual night to be slept (nox est perpetua una dormienda). Catullus uses the thought to urge love; Swinburne, after 'too much love of living', finds rest in it. The repetition 'eternal ... eternal' and the last masculine rhyme 'night' (with 'light' and 'sight') close the poem with finality, the culmination of its slow descent.
